issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on a presumption of death to establish a timely right to possession must prove the time of death when the limitation period depends on when that right accrued.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of ancestral property after obtaining a declaratory decree concerning an earlier alienation.
The right to seek possession accrued when the last owner died and the line of succession became extinct.
The last owner had not been heard of for more than seven years, but the plaintiffs did not prove when within that period he died.
The applicable limitation period for a possession suit following a declaratory decree was three years from accrual of the right to sue.
issues.conclusion: The presumption that the missing owner was dead did not establish the time of death. Because the plaintiffs did not prove that he died within three years before filing, they failed to establish that the suits were timely.
issues.legal_principle: Article 2(b) of the Schedule to the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 required suit within three years of accrual of the right to sue. Under section 108 of the Evidence Act, 1872, seven years without being heard of permits a presumption of death, but does not presume the precise time of death; a claimant whose right depends on death at a particular time must prove that timing. The Court relied on Nepean v. Doe D. Knight, Jayawant Jivarao Deshpande v. Ramachandra Narayan Joshi, Lalchand Marwari v. Ramrup Gir, Jiwan Singh v. Kuar Reoti Singh, Kottappalli Venkateswarlu v. Kottapalli Bapayya, Punjab v. Natha, and Ram Kali v. Narain Singh.

rule.if: ancestral_property_possession_suit_after_declaratory_decree and right_to_sue_depends_on_owner_death and owner_unheard_for_seven_years and not evidence_places_death_within_limitation_period

predicates.ancestral_property_possession_suit_after: The plaintiffs brought a possession suit concerning ancestral property after a declaratory decree had been obtained concerning its alienation.
predicates.right_to_sue_depends_on_owner_death: The plaintiffs’ right to seek possession depended on the last owner’s death and the resulting opening of succession.
predicates.owner_unheard_for_seven_years: The plaintiffs established that the owner had not been heard of for at least seven years by those who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive.
predicates.evidence_places_death_within_limitation_: The plaintiffs produced evidence establishing that the owner died within the period that would make the possession suit timely.

issues.definition: When a possession claim following a declaratory decree depends on the owner’s death, proof that the owner was unheard of for seven years establishes neither the time of death nor timeliness unless evidence places the death within the limitation period.

issues.legal_issue: Time spent pursuing an earlier civil proceeding is not excluded from limitation when the earlier court was able to entertain the suit and dismissed it as premature, or when the later proceeding is founded on a different cause of action.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had previously sued for possession based on an allegation that the last owner died on a particular date.
The earlier suits were dismissed as premature because the owner’s death had not been established.
The earlier court had jurisdiction and was not otherwise unable to entertain the suits.
The later suits relied on the owner having remained unheard of for seven years, a basis not available in the earlier suits.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs could not exclude the time spent in the earlier litigation under section 14(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908 requires, among other things, that the earlier proceeding be prosecuted in good faith in a court unable to entertain it because of a defect of jurisdiction or another cause of a like nature, and that both proceedings be founded on the same cause of action. Applying ejusdem generis, “other cause of a like nature” means a defect analogous to a jurisdictional defect that bars the court from entertaining the earlier suit. The Court relied on Bhai Jai Kishan Singh v. People Bank of Northern India, Dwarkanath Chakravarti v. Atul Chandra Chakravarti, and Palla Pattabhiramayya v. Velaga Narayana Rao.

rule.if: later_civil_proceeding_after_prior_civil_proceeding and ((prior_suit_dismissed_as_premature and prior_court_was_able_to_entertain) or not same_cause_of_action)

predicates.later_civil_proceeding_after_prior_civil: The plaintiffs brought a later civil proceeding after pursuing an earlier civil proceeding against the defendants.
predicates.prior_suit_dismissed_as_premature: The earlier court dismissed the suit because the asserted right to sue had not yet been established as having accrued.
predicates.prior_court_was_able_to_entertain: The earlier court had authority and capacity to consider the suit rather than being barred from entertaining it by a jurisdictional or analogous defect.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The earlier and later proceedings rested on the same essential facts constituting the plaintiffs’ asserted right to relief.

issues.definition: Time in an earlier proceeding is not excluded when the earlier court could entertain the suit despite dismissing it as premature, or when the later proceeding rests on a different cause of action.

issues.legal_issue: A later amendment removing rights to contest certain alienations does not defeat an appeal concerning an alienation protected by an unchanged saving provision.
material_facts: The appeals concerned an alienation made before the 1920 legislation came into force.
The 1973 amending legislation changed provisions governing the right to contest alienations but left the saving provision unchanged.
The saving provision preserved rights to contest alienations made before the original legislation came into force.
issues.conclusion: The 1973 amendment did not make the appeals untenable because the earlier alienation remained protected by the saving provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Act, 1920 preserved rights to contest an alienation made before that Act came into force. The 1973 amendment did not amend that saving provision; the Court also noted that the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 had not been repealed.

predicates.appeal_concerns_pre_existing_alienation: The appeal concerns an alienation made before the legislation that later regulated the right to contest alienations came into force.
predicates.saving_provision_preserves_pre_existing_: A saving provision preserves the right to contest an alienation made before that legislation came into force.
predicates.later_amendment_leaves_saving_provision_: A later amendment changes other provisions but does not alter the saving provision protecting the earlier right.

issues.definition: An appeal concerning an earlier alienation remains maintainable when a saving provision preserves the right at issue and a later amendment leaves that provision unchanged.
